perf-fluctuation deep dive · trace-sync-points session · probes v10 (tag 7600) + v10b (tags 7601+7600) · campaigns 3c51-fence3-tp4-20260813T050910Z and 3c51-fence13-tp4-20260813T060034Z · delphi-3c51 · 2026-08-13

Fences 1 and 3 measured: the definitive sync points bracket the lottery’s moving parts

The runbook question — does the C.rest stretch live in the wake at the definitive sync point, or in the next-step construction? — is answered, twice:

  • The wake [callback end → Fence 3] is flat in both campaigns: 23k → 22k cycles (corr +0.11) in campaign 1; 21k → 25k (corr -0.10) in campaign 2. The scheduler wake at the definitive sync point never tracks the lottery — the codex-F4-class suspect is excluded, replicated.
  • When C.rest stretches, the stretch is in [Fence 3 → end point] (the scheduler’s single-threaded next-step construction): campaign 1 saw C.rest grow +110k and construction carried 410k → 521k (corr -0.79) — essentially all of it. In campaign 2 the same segment grew only +27k (construction +24k, corr -0.43); that campaign’s lottery expressed elsewhere (next bullet).
  • New in campaign 2 (Fence 1, tag 7601): the 70-worker join convoy [window open → Fence 1] moves with the lottery — 526k → 702k cycles (+176k, corr -0.65), the largest child of that campaign’s span growth. The serial [Fence 1 → wcls dispatch] leg is small but the most tightly correlated child: 64k → 87k (corr -0.81).

The two campaigns, 50 minutes apart on the same host and binary lineage, distributed the span growth differently (campaign 1: fill-dominated; campaign 2: join-convoy-dominated) — consistent with the known co-stretch texture in which child shares vary per campaign while the span itself carries the difference (corr -0.89 and -0.86). corr here and everywhere below = Pearson correlation of the per-draw segment mean vs decode TPS across the campaign’s clean draws (−1 = longer exactly when slower, 0 = no relationship).

Two probe stamps at the token cycle’s two definitive sync points (see glossary), plus a dispatch cut derived from existing records:

  • Tag 7601 (campaign 2) brackets the workers_done.wait() join at generated qwen_3_4b_instruct_2507.hpp:6690–6692 (scheduler thread). Record end = Fence 1. Indexed by end timestamp in the analyzer — the scheduler can enter the join before worker 0’s layer-35 barrier release.
  • wcls dispatch cut: the first TX dispatch instant (tag 3000+dev) after Fence 1 — at Fence 1 the hardware pipeline is empty, so this is the wcls launch.

7.2 · Same token, both runs: is a slow token slow in both?

No — token identity does not set the span’s cost. Pairing the two runs at identical token positions: Pearson correlation between the two series is 0.20 and rank (Spearman) correlation is 0.06 — essentially unrelated token-by-token. Only 5 of each run’s 20 slowest positions coincide. The slowest run is slower at 64.2% of positions, by a median of 104k — a broad shift, not shared spikes; the per-position difference varies with a standard deviation of 930k, close to what fully independent draws would give (1,037k).

One structure does show up at the position level: the slow run drifts. Its rolling median climbs across the run — medians by position quarter 1,295k → 1,329k → 1,420k → 1,661k (+28.2% first-to-last) — while the fast run stays flat (1,260k → 1,287k, +2.2%). In the first quarter the runs are ~2.9% apart; by the last quarter, 29.0%. So “slow run” here means “a run whose [F1→F3] baseline degrades as the run progresses”, not “a run whose tokens are individually unlucky”. Hypothesis (labeled): a per-launch state that worsens either with elapsed time or with KV-cache growth. Within a run these are inseparable: at the near-constant ~170 tok/s decode rate, token position, elapsed time, and KV length (= prompt 1024 + prefix 256 + position) rise in lockstep, so the drift curve fits both equally well — and a longer gen-length would NOT separate them (same position↔time mapping; it only extends the curve, which answers saturation, not cause). The separating measurement is a prompt-length A/B: a +2,048-token prompt reaches any given KV size ~2,048 positions ≈ 12 s earlier in the run. KV-driven → the drift curve shifts left by ~2,048 positions (the run starts “pre-aged”); time-driven → the curve keeps its elapsed-time profile, offset only by the ~1 s longer prefill. Cheapest first check (analysis-only): whether the same drift appears in this campaign’s other 14 draws with amplitude tracking TPS. Both follow-ups have since been run: §7.2.1 (all-draw check) and §7.2.3 (the prompt-length A/B — verdict: absolute KV size excluded).

7.2.3 · The prompt-length A/B, done: absolute KV size is excluded

Design. Arm A = campaign 2 (prompt 1,024). Arm B = the same workload, binary (install-kvprobe10b), host and gates with prompt 3,072 (+2,048): campaign 3c51-fence13p3072-tp4-20260813T184426Z, smoke+16/16, prompt length verified in the recorded command line, token sha c91640a749da… identical ×17 (a new sequence, as a different prompt must produce), zero freeze holes, machine restored. TPS 139.221–149.402 — ≈14% below arm A, as expected from attention reading a larger KV. Arm B enters its first decode token at KV size 3,330 — the size arm A only reaches at position ≈2,048. If the §7.2.1 drift were driven by absolute KV size, arm B would start at arm A’s “aged” level and the two arms’ curves would form one function of KV. If it is anchored to run progress, the arms align at equal position instead.

On the KV axis the arms do NOT form one function: arm B re-enters at the baseline (its curves start at ≈1,267k) exactly where arm A’s drifted draws had climbed. Flat curves exist at every KV size in both arms — the baseline is attainable across the whole 1,282–7,424 KV range, so KV size does not force the elevation.

On the position axis the arms coincide at the baseline: group-median first-quarter levels 1,263k (arm A) vs 1,267k (arm B). In the equal-KV overlap, the group medians differ only marginally — and in the wrong direction for a KV effect (arm B lower):

This is the “fat mode” texture (a whole-run level shift, as in the 3bda ungated campaign) where arm A’s campaign expressed as a ramp — together with §7.2.2’s front-loaded convoy tax, the consistent reading is a per-launch state with variable onset and decay that is not a function of KV size. What would separate elapsed time from token-count within the progress family: an idle-pause mid-run or a decode-rate intervention; neither is supported by the current harness.

7.2.4 · The F1-window check, done: wcls never starts before Fence 1; the [open→F1] wait tracks trailing transfers

The question (owner follow-up on §7.2.2, 2026-08-13). Two readings of the §7.2.2 pair needed a direct test: (a) work that usually executes inside [F1→F3] might execute before F1 in some runs — the fences would then not partition work the same way in every run; (b) draw_01’s cheaper post-F1 legs might mean their input state was ready before F1 — sharpest version: the wcls stream launched before Fence 1, which would turn §7.2.2’s B-fill difference into a bookkeeping artifact of the wcls dispatch cut. Both are checkable from records already collected: the probe stamps every device dispatch (tag 3000+dev, tx_launch) and every rx completion (tag 4000+dev) as instants (h/system/kvwait_probe.hpp). Extraction: f1win_dump.py → per-token f1win-drawNN.csv, same 4,095-gap set as every other per-token series on this page.

Finding 1 — the wcls stream is never launched before Fence 1. Across all 16 draws (65,520 tokens), 18 tokens have any tx_launch within 50k cycles (19µs) of F1 — at most 3 per draw; draw_01 has 0, draw_06 has 2. The smallest dispatch→F1 gap anywhere is 38k. The first dispatch after F1 is therefore always the wcls launch: the wcls dispatch cut is valid, and draw_01’s cheaper B fill in §7.2.2 is a real post-F1 effect, not an early-launch artifact.

Finding 2 — the window is not idle, and its variable part is the trailing transfers. Every token carries ~13–14 trailing tx_launch dispatches and ~13 rx completions into the window (the tail of the forward pass’s transfer stream — the per-draw median offset of the first in-window dispatch from the window open is 1k–13k, a few percent of the window). The window splits into a transfer phase [open → last rx completion] and a quiet interval [last rx completion → F1] with no device traffic:

The quiet interval is nearly constant everywhere — 72k–92k (27µs–34µs) across all 16 draws, corr(quiet median, TPS) = -0.23 — while the transfer phase spans 164k–347k and carries the window differences: corr(transfer median, window median) = 0.93 across draws, corr(transfer median, TPS) = -0.64. For the §7.2.2 pair: window median 246k → 417k (+171k), transfer phase 164k → 347k (+183k), quiet interval 86k → 92k (+7k) — the pair’s whole [open→F1] difference is transfer-phase time. draw_01’s front-loaded decay (§7.2.2) also lives there: transfer-phase quarter medians 461k → 392k → 313k → 308k while draw_06 stays flat (160k–166k), and the stretch is uniform across the four devices (per-device last-rx medians 250k–330k vs 146k–152k).

Finding 3 — trailing rx completions do cross Fence 1, run-dependently. On 93.0% of draw_01’s tokens and 98.7% of draw_06’s, rx completions land between F1 and the wcls launch (median 2 per such token in draw_01, 4 in draw_06) — the sync-point survey’s “µs-scale trailing rx cleanup” exemption, now measured per token. A run whose join wait is short leaves more of the trailing completions on the far side of F1. This confirms reading (a) for device traffic — the fence slices the trailing transfer stream at a run-dependent point — but at instant-stamp magnitude, on the wcls-launch flank where nothing waits on it; no dispatch ever crosses.

Reading. Fence 1 fires a nearly fixed 72k–92k after the last trailing rx completion; what differs between launches — and what decays across draw_01’s run — is how long the trailing transfers keep arriving. So the [open→F1] wait is a drain of trailing device transfers, and §7.2.2’s launch difference is set in that drain. Open question (labeled hypothesis): whether the last workers wait on the trailing transfers or produce them — the rx stamps carry no issuer identity. Direct next measurements: the per-worker count-down stamps of section 11 (which worker is last, same seat or not), and a gated perfetto capture over [window open → last rx] with scheduler wake-chain events (sched_waking: who woke whom). Both are host-side views; if the trailing transfers are late because a device services them late, the host trace shows only the late arrival — device-side counters would be the follow-up there.

7.2.5 · Same functions between the fences? SQL recipes, UI walk-through, and the boundary-crossing inventory

All of the following runs against the traced campaign fence13pf-tp4-20260813T210954Z (17 captures: smoke + 16 draws, the "fence 1"/ "fence 3" instants of the v11 build) with /scratch/jhan/tools/trace_processor query -f <file> <trace>, one statement per file, or pasted one at a time into the perfetto UI's Query (SQL) page. Statements S1+S2 build the window table (~2 s); S3/S4 are range joins (~40 s each on a 55 MB capture). Membership definition for S3: a span belongs to the window it starts in; spans crossing a fence are inventoried separately by S4.

CREATE PERFETTO TABLE fence_seq AS
SELECT ts, name,
       LEAD(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS next_ts,
       LEAD(name) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS next_name
FROM slice WHERE name IN ('fence 1','fence 3');
CREATE PERFETTO TABLE win AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS win_ix,
       ts, next_ts - ts AS dur
FROM fence_seq WHERE name = 'fence 1' AND next_name = 'fence 3';
-- same-set check: how many windows does each function start in?
SELECT s.name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT w.win_ix) AS windows_with_it,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM win) AS total_windows
FROM win w JOIN slice s
  ON s.ts >= w.ts AND s.ts < w.ts + w.dur
WHERE s.name NOT IN ('fence 1','fence 3')
GROUP BY s.name ORDER BY windows_with_it ASC;

Result — the same-set question, across all 17 captures: the function set starting inside [F1→F3] is the same everywhere. 10 names are present in 100% of windows in every capture; the full inventory:

The only below-1% names are end-of-run one-offs (Gen complete) — e.g. "Gen complete" appears in exactly one window per capture: the final generated token. There is no draw-dependent appearance or disappearance of functions inside the span; what varies is durations (§7.2.1–7.2.4, and the named-span analysis in deep-dive-3bda/2026-08-13-09-3bda-fence-spans.html). Caveats: track-event names, not sampled symbols; spans with dur = −1 (unfinished at capture end, ~13.6k/trace) are excluded; the emission gate records events only between window open (layer-35 barrier end) and the next layer-0 entry, so work outside that region is invisible by design.

Perfetto UI walk-through — locating a window that contains a function which normally does not run in the span:

  1. Open https://ui.perfetto.dev → "Open trace file" → pick a capture (e.g. …/fence13pf-tp4-20260813T210954Z/results/draw_01/trace.pftrace, 55 MB loads in-browser). For remote files: /scratch/jhan/tools/trace_processor --httpd <trace> on alpha, then "Connect to trace_processor (RPC)" in the UI.
  2. Left sidebar → Query (SQL). Run S1, then S2, then S3. Rare names sit at the top of S3's output (ORDER BY windows_with_it ASC).
  3. Run S5 with the rare name (worked example: 'Gen complete' in draw_01 returns win_ix 3,875, slice_id 914013, thread 25/0-worker, dur 221 µs). Click the slice_id cell — the UI selects that slice on the timeline; press f to zoom to it.
  4. Orient yourself: press / and search fence 1 — the fences are zero-duration instants on the scheduler thread track (24/…-work_queue under the runtron process; Enter cycles matches). Pin the tracks you care about with the pin icon: the scheduler thread, 25/0-worker (fill/callback), the TX and RX driver threads.
  5. Read the window's function inventory directly: drag-select the region between the "fence 1" instant and the next "fence 3" instant across the pinned tracks — the selection panel at the bottom aggregates every slice in range by name (count + total duration). Compare against a neighboring window's selection to see what is extra or missing.
  6. Keys: W/S zoom, A/D pan, F zoom-to-selection, M mark the selected area.

The boundary-crossing inventory (S4), across all 17 captures. These are the spans that overlap a fence instant — they quantify exactly the exemptions in the fences' definitive-sync-point definitions (RX poll loops at F1; next-pass dispatch and µs-scale RX cleanup at F3).

-- boundary crossers: spans overlapping F1 or F3
SELECT s.name,
       SUM(s.ts < w.ts AND s.ts + s.dur <= w.ts + w.dur) AS f1_cross_end_inside,
       SUM(s.ts + s.dur > w.ts + w.dur) AS f3_cross,
       COUNT(*) AS crossing_pairs
FROM win w JOIN slice s
  ON s.dur > 0
 AND s.ts + s.dur >= w.ts
 AND s.ts < w.ts + w.dur
 AND (s.ts < w.ts OR s.ts + s.dur > w.ts + w.dur)
GROUP BY s.name ORDER BY crossing_pairs DESC;

S5-style locator queries (swap the name) jump to any instance.

Reconciling §7.2.4 finding 3 with the fences' “definitive” label (owner discussion, 2026-08-13). “Definitive sync point” bundles three claims of different strength, and keeping them separate removes the apparent contradiction between “F1 is definitive” and “things cross F1”:

tierclaim at F1status
1 · exact time cutone well-defined instant on the scheduler thread; attribution segments tile around it with zero residual true unconditionally — never required quiescence
2 · host program orderno host work crosses F1: all 70 workers joined, no listener exists yet, no tx dispatch crosses it proven (§7.2.4: 18 of 65,520 tokens with a tx_launch within 50k cycles ≈ zero; this table: tx_launch F1-crossings ending inside = 0 in all 17 captures)
3 · hardware quiet“the hardware pipeline is empty at F1” approximate — refined by §7.2.4 finding 3, see below

§7.2.4 finding 3 measured that the tier-3 exemption (“µs-scale trailing rx cleanup”) is not vacuous: real transfer completions trail past F1 (2–4 per token in 93–98.7% of tokens). Whether that breaks the label depends on whether those trailing completions are genuinely cleanup — nothing after F1 consumes them, and the exemption holds in spirit — or carry data that later work depends on, in which case the “full” label over-claims. That is exactly the open question §7.2.4 sharpened: who produces and who consumes the trailing transfers. Until it is answered, the honest statement is: F1 is proven definitive for host program order, and approximately definitive for hardware, with a measured, bounded exception that is itself the current investigation target. The span crossings in the tables above add no further violations: the crossing spans are poll/wait wrappers (tier-3 exemption by construction), the scheduler’s own enclosing span, or gate-split artifacts — and finding 3 itself was only measurable because tier 1 holds.

Artifact rows, verified as such: the kernel-named entries (kernel_rmsnorm_rope_rmsnorm_rope, Save K, and 3 instances of kernel_index_rmsnorm) are gate-split slices, not real cross-fence execution. In the gated captures their durations are multi-millisecond (Save K 4,100–6,816 µs; the rope kernel averages 3,679 µs, one instance even negative) while genuine kernels are µs-scale (kernel_index_rmsnorm averages 2 µs) — a begin emitted in one gate-open window paired with an end in a later one bridges the closed-gate region, the unmatched-END inflation documented on the pfgate pages. Only the driver and scheduler spans above physically cross the fences.

7.3 · Where the 841k-per-token difference lives — and what “48.3%” means

The two runs differ by 841k cycles per token (measured Fence-3→Fence-3 period means; the TPS-derived value agrees: 841k). A token cycle divides into four regions along the scheduler timeline — the forward pass (layer-0 Q-wait → layer-35 barrier) and the three fence-cut segments of the inter-fwd-pass span. Every region is slower in the slow run; the diagram shows both cycles to scale, then the difference tiled by region:

Lane diagram caption: durations to scale from the two draws’ mean segments; single scheduler-timeline lane per run (concurrent TX/RX/card work not shown — see the stall-map page for the multi-thread view); the difference bar is ×10 zoomed for readability.

Reading the shares: the percentages tile the difference between the runs, not the token’s time. The forward-pass region contributes 48.3% of the difference simply because it is huge (13,200k of a 15,581k cycle = 84.7% of the token): it slowed by only 3.1% of itself, yet that small relative slowdown is 406k in absolute terms. The inter-fwd-pass span is the concentrated part: it slowed by 18.3% of itself — about 6× the forward region’s relative slowdown — and its three fence-cut children [open→F1] +193k (22.9%), [F1→F3] +196k (23.3%), [F3→end] +45k (5.4%) tile the span’s 51.7% exactly.

Caveat: this is a single pair of draws. The campaign-level fast4/slow4 attribution (section 5) puts the forward region at 35.6% for campaign 2 — pair comparisons are noisier, and the forward-vs-span split itself varies with the draw pair chosen. The stable facts remain: the span concentrates the slowdown relative to its size, and the wake at Fence 3 stays flat.

10 · Glossary

inter-fwd-pass span
the once-per-token span from the layer-35 attention barrier end to the next pass’s layer-0 Q-wait entry (the span end point). Carries most of the launch difference on this host (this page §5; kvprobe7–9 campaigns).
definitive sync point
an instant every operation on every thread is definitively before or after — nothing concurrent with it (CS equivalents: quiescent point, BSP barrier). Used here in three tiers of strength (adopted 2026-08-13, see §7.2.5): tier 1 = an exact time cut (always true of the fences; all attribution rests on this); tier 2 = definitive for host program order (proven for F1: workers joined, no dispatch crosses it); tier 3 = hardware quiet (approximate at F1 — trailing transfer completions cross it, §7.2.4 finding 3, significance open; not claimed at F3, where next-pass TX work is concurrent by design). The strict textbook definition is unsatisfiable in this pipeline — RX pollers spin continuously — hence the stated exemption for idle/poll loops. The token cycle has two such instants, Fence 1 and Fence 3; the span end point is not one — TX threads already run next-pass work there.
Fence 1 / tag 7601
the scheduler’s join on all 70 pool workers (workers_done.wait() in the generated plugin’s run()); at its return the hardware pipeline is empty (wcls not yet launched). The record’s end is the fence timestamp.
Fence 3 / tag 7600
the scheduler’s wait for all logits listeners to acknowledge the token callback (listeners_notified.wait()); the record’s end is the fence timestamp, its start ≈ fence-2 (logits_done) return.
join convoy [open→F1]
from the layer-35 barrier end to Fence 1: the tail of the 70-worker join (workers finishing layer-35 tail work, retiring, counting down) — codex finding F1’s convoy, measured per token for the first time here.
wcls dispatch cut
the first TX dispatch instant (tag 3000+dev) after Fence 1, used as the wcls launch timestamp; valid because the pipeline is empty at Fence 1.
fast4 / slow4
the 4 highest-TPS / 4 lowest-TPS clean draws of a campaign.
corr
Pearson correlation of a per-draw segment mean vs decode TPS across clean draws; −1 = longer exactly when slower, 0 = no relationship.
C.rest (kvprobe7 term)
token-callback end → span end point; split by Fence 3 into cb→F3 and F3→end.
Fence-3→Fence-3 period
one complete token cycle between consecutive Fence-3 timestamps. NOT the inter-fwd-pass span. Exactly measured per token; the measured cross-check (and recommended future replacement) for the TPS-derived level-1 denominator.
codex F1, codex F4
findings from an external source review of the decode synchronization code (deep-dive/from-codex/decode-sync-source-review.md). F1 = the 70-worker listener fanout and pool-join structure — its join convoy is what [open→F1] measures here. F4 = a doorbell implemented as a plain volatile flag with a polling retry bound — the class of “wake latency at a sync point” suspects that the cb→F3 measurement tests (and excludes).
pfgate
the 2026-08-12 gated-perfetto campaign on delphi-3bda (20 draws; report in deep-dive-3bda/), which showed pure host compute such as compute_forward_args running ×3–5 slower inside stalled windows at constant clock.

11 · Next steps

Update 2026-08-14: the wcls-bypass A/B (status_report/2026-08-13-03-wcls-bypass.html) has since ruled out the wcls/fill pipeline as the jitter source: pinning fill_logits_buffer to a constant 2.5 ms leaves the per-token period spread at 99% of control and decorrelates [F1→F3] from TPS (−0.86 → −0.06) — the [F1→F3] window absorbs the jitter but does not create it; the source sits in the forward pass and the transfer phase. The fill-side items below (per-block arrival pacing) are therefore demoted from cause-hunting to symptom characterization; the forward-pass/transfer-phase items take priority. Also: delphi-3c51 was returned to its owner on 2026-08-14 — new campaigns run elsewhere.

  • Why does the [open→F1] join wait stretch? It is the largest measured mover in campaign 2 (+176k, corr -0.65). Candidate next probe: per-worker count-down stamps (which of the 70 workers is late, and is it the same seat every time?) — connects to codex F1’s fanout finding (chunk=1 collapsed fill-stall rates on 3bda but left the TPS lottery intact).
  • To-do (lower priority): settle the F1 tier-3 question from §7.2.5 — determine whether the trailing rx completions that cross F1 are consumed by any later work (then the “hardware quiet” claim over-reaches) or are pure cleanup (then the exemption holds in spirit). Largely subsumed by the trailing-transfers producer/consumer measurement from §7.2.4; keep as a named check so the fence terminology gets closed out either way.
  • Drill inside F3→end (campaign 1’s carrier): per-callee stamps around extend_request, compute_forward_args, construct_minibatches, plan assembly, and the layer-0 enqueue on the scheduler thread. pfgate already showed compute_forward_args ×3–5 inside stalled windows at constant clock.
  • [F1→wcls] as a cheap high-signal probe: tiny (64k → 87k) but corr -0.81 — the strongest child correlation in campaign 2. It is pure scheduler serial work (enqueue wcls + listener prep), a clean per-token proxy of the shared slow-down factor.
  • Adopt the F3→F3 period as the standard per-token denominator in level-1 tables, and for token-by-token reconciliation and exact freeze detection.
